segments.say: And now, very gently, the snow and the window seat and the valley all begin to fade, the way the last page of a favorite book fades when you turn out the light. And you find that you're somewhere familiar. A small, quiet kitchen, at the end of an ordinary evening, with the dishes put away and a single lamp left on.

It's Ines's kitchen, the one we began in. The radio on the windowsill is switched off. The plates are dry on the rack, and the cup of tea has long gone cold. She's gone up to bed, and the house is still, with the soft, ticking silence of a home at night.

The lamp throws a small circle of warm light over the table. Beyond it, the window shows a dark blue night, with a few stars, and the outline of a neighbor's roof. Nothing in the room is moving. Everything is where it should be, and everything is at rest.

Upstairs, Ines is lying in bed, with the covers drawn up, and her hair spread on the pillow. She's been thinking about her song, and the key change, and her cousin in the back of the car. And somewhere in the middle of one of those thoughts, without noticing, she's fallen asleep.

Her face is calm, and her breathing is slow and even. A faint trace of a smile rests on her lips, as though some small, good thing had just happened, which in a way it had. All evening, she's been a person who noticed that a few seconds of sound could make her whole body shiver, and who found that remarkable and lovely.

Tomorrow, she'll probably forget most of the science. The names, and the years, and the scans. But she may keep a small piece of it. That the shiver isn't random. That it's a reward, and a conversation between her expectations and the world, and one of the many ways a mind says, this matters.
And perhaps that's enough to carry away. A shiver is the body noticing that something is beautiful.

show.text: A shiver is the body noticing that something is beautiful.

segments.say: And you, too, can carry that with you into sleep, or simply let it go. You don't need to remember a single fact. The ideas will be there, if you ever want them. All that matters now is that your body is heavy, and your breath is slow, and your mind is soft.

Say goodnight, in your mind, to the whole day. To the people in it, and the sounds you heard, and the songs you hummed, and the quiet moments between. To the good parts, and the hard parts, and the parts in between. They've all been part of a day that's now complete.

Take one more slow, full breath, in through your nose, and out through your mouth, and let it carry away anything that remains. And now, let your breathing go back to its own quiet pace, the one it knows, without any help from you.
The night is long, and gentle, and kind. It has all the time in the world, and it will keep you safe, and it will give you back in the morning, rested, and a little lighter than you were.

There is nothing left to do, and nowhere left to go. Your body is resting. Your mind is quiet. The soft dark is warm around you. And in a moment, or in a few, you won't even notice that you've stopped listening.

And next time, if you'd like to join me again, we'll explore another very human puzzle. Why does your mind keep drifting away from what you're doing, to the past, the future and a hundred small imaginings, and what does science say about where it goes? I'll see you then.
